routes.description: Psychophysical harmony favors theism over naturalism because value-supporting relations between phenomenal and physical or functional states are antecedently much less expected without a value-selecting creator.
routes.successCriteria: Establish identifiable harmony data and a warranted comparative likelihood claim under which those data are substantially more expected on theism than on relevant naturalist alternatives.

motionBridge.description: Psychophysical harmony supplies substantial evidence for God over naturalism.

centralBridges.description: Actual psychophysical relations exhibit significant normative or semantic harmony and enable consciousness-involving goods.
Harmony is antecedently unlikely on naturalism across relevant psychophysical possibilities, including simple alternatives.
A perfectly good creator makes value-supporting psychophysical relations more expected.
The evidential comparison can survive identity theory when a substantial epistemic gap remains between physical and phenomenal truths.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Evolution does not independently explain why phenomenal qualities have their actual normative roles.
A comparative likelihood judgment may be warranted without precise numerical probabilities or a unique measure.

routes.description: Harmony does not establish the proposed evidential advantage because identity naturalism removes the contingent correlation, the relevant probability measure is unsupported, and theism's comparative fit is not independently secured.
routes.successCriteria: Show that at least one indispensable likelihood bridge fails for a serious naturalist view or that the comparative evidential claim lacks a justified measure or theistic fit.

motionBridge.description: The presented harmony considerations do not establish evidence for God over naturalism.

centralBridges.description: On identity naturalism, phenomenal and neural events are one event rather than separately correlated items requiring psychophysical selection.
Pain's causal and rationalizing relation to aversive behavior may be knowable a priori, undermining purported inversion possibilities.
No justified probability measure over psychophysical possibilities has been supplied for the likelihood comparison.
A complete theory comparison must assess simplicity and all salient fit data, including suffering that creates pressure for perfect-good theism.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Pain itself participates in causing aversive behavior, contrary to epiphenomenalist presentations.
Identity need only be token identity, with restricted type identities left open by neuroscience.

sections.title: The harmony datum and the identity alternative
sections.rationale: This issue fixes what requires explanation and whether the central datum is a contingent mapping at all.

proMoves.speaker: Brian Cutter
proMoves.proposition: The normative alignment between pain's badness and its avoidance role is striking because many conceivable psychophysical mappings would invert or neutralize phenomenal value while leaving behavior disharmonious.

sourceSpan.excerpt: normative harmony ... consists in the fact that ... the normative roles of experiences are aligned with their descriptive or functional roles

proMoves.attributionBasis: Continuous opening statement explicitly assigned to Brian Cutter by the moderator.

response.rationale: This is the initial constructive specification of the harmony datum and has no earlier selected target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Normative harmony is defined through descriptive and normative roles, and the inversion comparison is expressly bounded to alternative psychophysical regimes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples make disharmonious alternatives intelligible, but do not by themselves establish their prevalence under a justified measure.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inversion and neutral-sensation cases form a stable contrast, though the transition from conceivable alternatives to strikingness retains an implicit modal-distribution bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Concrete counterfactual mappings support the datum, but their representativeness among relevant possibilities is not independently established.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly develops the assigned datum without depending on an earlier exchange.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially establishes the pro route's central data bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: No live opponent alternative is represented in this span.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Brian defines normative harmony, develops pain/pleasure inversion and neutral-experience cases, and argues that evolution presupposes rather than explains the relevant alignment.

conMoves.speaker: Graham Oppy
conMoves.proposition: On identity naturalism, pain experiences just are neural events that cause and rationalize aversive behavior, so there are not two items whose correlation calls for psychophysical selection or explanation.

sourceSpan.excerpt: phenomenal events, pain events for example, just are neural events ... there isn't a question about correlation that arises

conMoves.attributionBasis: Continuous opening response explicitly handed to Graham Oppy.

response.rationale: Although contrary to the preceding opening, this is Oppy's independently developed constructive route and is recorded without a response target.

precisionFindings.rationale: Oppy identifies event identity, distinguishes it from correlation, and limits the proposal at minimum to token identity.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The identity thesis yields the claimed consequence if true, but its truth is asserted rather than established; Oppy acknowledges uncertainty about type identities.

charity.alternative: Cutter's argument treats phenomenal and physical states as distinct relata linked by psychophysical laws.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cutter presents property dualism as a substantial and controversial starting assumption that he thinks may later be relaxed.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The Venus analogy clearly explains why strict identity would dissolve a correlation question; whether identity is true is evidential rather than inferential.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The position is supported by a coherent identity model and causal intuition, but receives little independent defense against the explanatory-gap considerations.

responsiveness.rationale: As a constructive opening, it directly establishes the con route's principal alternative.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central characterization of harmony as a contingent psychophysical mapping.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy accurately recognizes that Cutter's initial argument assumes distinct phenomenal properties and notes that the argument may affect other naturalisms.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Oppy states event identity, uses the Hesperus/Phosphorus analogy, argues that pain participates in causing behavior, and expressly leaves restricted type identities open.

sections.title: Whether the argument survives materialism
sections.rationale: The exchange tests whether the pro case reaches Oppy's adopted naturalism rather than only property-dualist naturalism.

proMoves.speaker: Brian Cutter
proMoves.proposition: Identity does not by itself defeat the evidential argument: if physical and phenomenal truths remain epistemically separable, harmony can still be comparatively likely on theism even if the properties are metaphysically identical.

sourceSpan.excerpt: identity theory is true ... doesn't necessarily affect the probabilities at all ... here we're talking about epistemic probabilities

proMoves.attributionBasis: Moderator hands the identity question to Brian, followed by uninterrupted first-person argument.

components.text: Address whether identity removes any separate correlation or explanatory target.
Supply a reason to accept an epistemic gap or reject Oppy's a priori identity-naturalist alternative.

response.rationale: Cutter explains how an epistemic likelihood question can remain despite metaphysical identity, but does not yet establish that Oppy's own view contains the required gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply distinguishes explanatory from probabilistic formulations and conditions its reach on type-B materialism or an epistemic gap.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Cutter repeatedly concedes that materialism makes the terrain trickier and presents survival of the argument conditionally.

charity.alternative: Oppy's identity theory says pain and its neural realization are a single event, eliminating a correlation between distinct entities.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy leaves unsettled whether his identity theory is a priori physicalism or instead permits a physical-phenomenal epistemic gap.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The epistemic/metaphysical distinction supplies a coherent route around the identity objection, with the applicability to Oppy's exact view unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The reply identifies a recognized physicalist distinction but does not independently defend the epistemic gap within the selected span.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive identity consequence but leaves the evidential case against Oppy's specific a priori alternative unfinished.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially advances the central bridge extending the argument to materialism.

representationalCharity.rationale: Cutter expressly grants that identities do not call for explanation and carefully isolates the remaining epistemic issue.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Cutter concedes that identities need no explanation, reformulates the case probabilistically, and conditions its materialist extension on an epistemic rather than ontological gap.

conMoves.speaker: Graham Oppy
conMoves.proposition: Pain's causal and rationalizing connection to aversive behavior may be knowable a priori, making inversion scenarios and the claimed epistemic gap doubtful rather than available merely because formal logic permits them.

sourceSpan.excerpt: I think that it's just a priori that pain unlike pleasure causes and rationalizes aversive behavior

conMoves.attributionBasis: Speaker transition and the content track Oppy's first-person defense of his identity view.

components.text: Address whether an epistemic gap remains between complete physical information and phenomenal truths.
Resolve how the a priori pain-role claim identifies particular phenomenal states from complete physical information.

response.rationale: Oppy supplies an a priori role constraint relevant to the gap but remains unsure how fully it closes Cutter's proposed physical-to-phenomenal deduction gap.

precisionFindings.rationale: The pain-role generic is clear, but its scope from a behavioral constraint to complete phenomenal deduction remains unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy strongly endorses the a priori generic while openly expressing uncertainty about conceivability and the precise epistemic-gap classification.

charity.alternative: Cutter distinguishes metaphysical identity from an epistemic gap that could sustain comparative likelihoods.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cutter's route requires a substantive gap from complete physical information to phenomenal truths, not merely different vocabularies.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The a priori pain-role claim bears on inversion, but it does not fully entail the denial of every relevant physical-phenomenal epistemic gap.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The causal-role intuition is plausible, yet the a priori status and its extension to phenomenal identity receive limited defense.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the decisive gap issue while leaving the complete-deduction challenge unresolved.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro route's central materialism bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy engages the epistemic-gap proposal as stated, though his response sometimes moves toward the narrower claim about pain's functional role.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Oppy distinguishes mere logical consistency from substantive epistemic possibility and invokes an a priori connection between pain and aversive behavior, while acknowledging uncertainty about the resulting classification.

sections.title: Theistic expectation and comparative theory fit
sections.rationale: Even if harmony is special, the motion requires a comparative bridge showing that God makes it more expected without ignoring contrary fit data.

proMoves.speaker: Brian Cutter
proMoves.proposition: Harmony is more expected on theism because a perfectly good and powerful creator would act for valuable states of affairs, and actual psychophysical laws enable consciousness-involving goods far better than salient alternatives.

sourceSpan.excerpt: given that the being is perfectly good ... we would kind of expect it to act for the sake of the good

proMoves.attributionBasis: Closing portion of Brian Cutter's uninterrupted opening statement.

response.rationale: This is the opening motion-level likelihood comparison and has no selected response target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is explicitly between theism and naturalism and is tied to specified consciousness-involving goods.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Perfect goodness supplies a recognizable value-selection warrant, but the move does not fully address competing divine reasons or the world's mixed value profile.

charity.alternative: Naturalism may favor simple laws rather than a flat distribution over every conceivable psychophysical mapping.
charity.decisiveQualification: The naturalist simplicity response need not claim that every simple law is harmonious, only that the relevant prior is not established by counting possibilities.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The value-selection inference is intelligible and connected to the listed goods, with divine choice and competing-value bridges compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies concrete goods and examines simple naturalist alternatives, but offers limited support for the comparative magnitude of the likelihoods.

responsiveness.rationale: As an opening constructive, it clearly advances the complete motion-level conclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It expressly supports the complete evidential conclusion that harmony favors theism over naturalism.

representationalCharity.rationale: Cutter anticipates a simplicity-based naturalist prior, although he mainly tests it against a limited family of simple laws.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Cutter summarizes the harmony data, argues that zombie and simple particle-experience laws do not yield the goods, and connects perfect goodness to value-realizing creation.

conMoves.speaker: Graham Oppy
conMoves.proposition: Theory comparison must include simplicity and the full fit of each theory to the data; extensive apparently purposeless animal suffering creates explanatory pressure for a perfectly good God and can make naturalism comparatively simpler.

sourceSpan.excerpt: what was attractive about this to God? Why did God choose to make a world with 500 million years of animal suffering that really doesn't seem to serve any purpose?

conMoves.attributionBasis: Oppy's sustained first-person answer in the moderated discussion is distinguishable from the moderator's prompts.

components.text: Address whether perfect goodness makes the observed value-supporting harmony more expected.
Compare the specific psychophysical harmony datum under theism and naturalism rather than substituting an overall argument from evil.

response.rationale: The suffering evidence challenges the simple goodness-to-fit inference and broadens theory comparison appropriately, but does not directly calculate or defeat the likelihood of harmony itself.

precisionFindings.rationale: Oppy distinguishes intuitive explanatory comparison from Bayesian formulation and limits his example to comparative fit and theoretical commitments.

calibrationFindings.rationale: He presents the suffering objection as pressure rather than a conclusive refutation and acknowledges skeptical-theist responses.

charity.alternative: Cutter argues that a perfectly good creator would have reason to realize consciousness-involving goods through harmonious laws.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cutter claims comparative evidential support from harmony, not that harmony alone establishes the best complete worldview or a perfect world.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand to compare total fit and complexity is coherent, though the move shifts from the local likelihood to wider worldview evidence.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The long history of animal suffering is a concrete rival datum, but its net bearing depends on disputed theistic explanations.

responsiveness.rationale: It contacts the goodness-based expectation but does not fully answer the specific likelihood comparison for harmony.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It materially attacks the central bridge from divine goodness to expected psychophysical harmony.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy recognizes the value-based theistic explanation and allows that skeptical-theist replies may be acceptable, while correctly treating the issue as broader fit.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Oppy contrasts naturalistic unfolding and evolution with theistic reasons for prolonged animal suffering, then argues that added auxiliary commitments count against theoretical simplicity.

sections.title: Comparative probabilities without a natural measure
sections.rationale: The evidential conclusion depends on whether qualitative likelihood comparisons are warranted when precise priors and a measure over possible laws are unavailable.

proMoves.speaker: Brian Cutter
proMoves.proposition: A qualitative likelihood ratio can be strongly warranted without numerical probabilities or a unique measure, as message-like arrangements plainly favor agency over chance across reasonable measures.

sourceSpan.excerpt: what matters at the end of the day is that we can be justified in thinking that one probability is significantly higher than another

proMoves.attributionBasis: The moderator's question is followed by Brian's extended first-person defense and design analogies.

components.text: Show that epistemic comparative probabilities need not reduce to mere compatibility with logic or require exact numerical values.
Supply a non-question-begging measure or dominance argument specifically for psychophysical laws.

response.rationale: The analogies defend qualitative epistemic probability in principle, but do not fully transfer a measure-independent dominance result to harmony.

precisionFindings.rationale: Cutter clearly limits the claim to comparative likelihood and openly disclaims precise numbers and a uniquely natural measure.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The message analogies strongly support qualitative comparisons in some cases, but the assertion that any reasonable measure favors theism for harmony is insufficiently demonstrated.

charity.alternative: Oppy worries that epistemic probabilities lack rational grounding when no objective chance or defensible measure over possibilities is available.
charity.decisiveQualification: Oppy allows subjective or ignorance-managing probabilities in structured cases and chiefly challenges what fixes them here.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between exact values and robust comparative ordering is sound, but transfer from visibly message-like data to psychophysical harmony needs another bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The leaf-message and inscribed-atom examples make the general point vivid, while the relevant law-space comparison remains asserted.

responsiveness.rationale: The move rebuts the demand for precise numbers but does not fully answer the missing-measure challenge for the actual datum.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It advances the necessary subsidiary probability bridge rather than independently completing the motion.

representationalCharity.rationale: Cutter explicitly grants Oppy's technical concerns about infinite spaces and unavailable precise assignments before identifying the narrower comparative claim.

proMoves.evidenceBasis: Cutter distinguishes qualitative likelihood ordering from exact probability assignment and uses leaves spelling a message and inscriptions inside atoms as agency-over-chance analogies.

conMoves.speaker: Graham Oppy
conMoves.proposition: Where neither hypothesis dominates in both simplicity and data fit, the Bayesian formulation requires at least rough justified weighting; otherwise it is unclear how to trade naturalism's simplicity against theism's alleged better fit.

sourceSpan.excerpt: maybe you do think naturalism is simpler but theism fits the data much better ... it's hard to know how to weigh that up

conMoves.attributionBasis: Direct speaker response following Brian's probability analogies, with Oppy's characteristic first-person qualifications.

components.text: Address whether qualitative comparisons can avoid exact numerical assignments.
Explain why the harmony comparison still needs justified weighting when simplicity and fit point in opposite directions.

response.rationale: Oppy grants dominance cases without numbers and isolates why Cutter's nondominance comparison still needs a warranted tradeoff.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply carefully distinguishes dominance cases from cases where prior simplicity and likelihood fit conflict.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Oppy makes the bounded claim that weighting is hard without rough numbers, not that all qualitative probability judgments are illegitimate.

charity.alternative: Cutter claims that robust qualitative likelihood inequalities can be obvious despite unavailable exact values and nonunique measures.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cutter does not claim that theism has a higher prior and concedes that naturalism may be simpler.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The dominance/nondominance distinction directly identifies when qualitative ordering suffices and when a tradeoff remains.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is analytically well supported by Cutter's own concession about priors, though it does not prove that no rough weighting can be justified.

responsiveness.rationale: It answers both the no-numbers analogy and the decisive application problem by distinguishing dominance from conflicting theoretical virtues.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the central claim that harmony is established as unlikely on naturalism relative to theism.

representationalCharity.rationale: Oppy preserves Cutter's strongest point that numerical precision is unnecessary in dominance cases and targets only the unresolved tradeoff.

conMoves.evidenceBasis: Oppy accepts ratio and dominance reasoning when simplicity and fit favor the same view, then notes that Cutter concedes no higher theistic prior and lacks a way to weigh opposing virtues.

pro.rationale: No distinct debate-wide consequence remains outside the selected move ratings, response links, importance assignments, section weights, and route analysis.

eligibility.completionCriterion: Establish that harmony is substantially more expected on theism than on relevant naturalist alternatives.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: None beyond the represented disputes over identity, theistic fit, and comparative probability.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the alleged residual consequence would not alter burden completion independently of fields already scored.

con.rationale: All debate-wide consequences of the identity, a priori-role, comparative-fit, and probability objections are already captured in selected moves and their structural fields.

eligibility.completionCriterion: Show failure of an indispensable likelihood bridge for the presented pro argument.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: None separate from the objections represented and rated in the four contested sections.
eligibility.counterfactual: No independently unscored consequence would change whether the con success criterion was met.
